I ordered these hoping they would solve a simple problem: comfortable, well-fitting sports gloves for weekend rides. What arrived was a disappointment from the moment I opened the package. The sizing chart must be a bad joke — despite ordering my usual size and measuring my hands according to their instructions, the gloves are unwearable. The fingers are either too tight or too long in weird places, and the thumb seam sits in the wrong spot, making every grip awkward.

Material feels cheaper than advertised. The fabric claims breathability but my hands felt clammy after just twenty minutes of use. The padding is uneven and seems to bunch up after minimal movement. The wrist closure is flimsy; the Velcro barely holds, and after a few stretches it was already fraying. I used them only twice and that was enough. For the price, I expected better durability and fit.

Customer service was also not helpful. I reached out about an exchange and got a canned response that didn’t address the sizing issue or offer a prepaid return. Between the poor fit, subpar materials, and lackluster support, this product didn’t meet basic expectations.

If you’re looking for reliable gloves for cycling, hiking, or general outdoor use, look elsewhere. Don’t waste your money on these — unless you enjoy fiddling with ill-fitting gear and spending extra time and money to return it. I’ll be buying a different brand and I recommend you do the same.

title: Not Indestructible, but a Great Value
text:
Our shiba loves these toys. For small dogs (20-25lbs), shibas are notoriously rough and tumble players, with the ability to tear through a cold turkey in a matter of minutes (or so one popular breeder/trainer attests from personal experience). So, imagine what they can do to their toys!

Our girl is relatively (key word, here!) calm for a shiba. She never touches anything that isn't hers, but she can get the crazies and do a number on her toys. Tug-of-war is her davorite game, after all, and these are made for it. So, the fact that these are stuffingless is reassuring. She will sometimes tear the ears off of the foxes, but it's from over-time wear-and-tear. She will eventually rip the giant one up (high-energy breeds of any size above a toy breed will need the jumbo), but it will last long enough to be worth the ten or so dollars.

Bottom line, I very much recommend these for all but the most destructive of dogs. The only reason I am not giving five stars is due to the fact that they do eventually wear down, but the low price makes this tolerable. The only other critique I have is that the animal you get seems random, with no visible way to request one over another (our girl really prefers the fox).

title: Don't buy this item
text:
I really wanted to like this, but after spending an afternoon trying to make it work, I have to warn everyone: do not waste your money. The box art looked fantastic, and the description promised hours of creative play for my seven-year-old. In reality, the product is a complete mess.

First, the pieces are cut from the thinnest, cheapest cardboard I have ever seen. They started peeling and bending the moment we tried to punch them out. Several of the interlocking tabs snapped off before we even assembled the first section. The instructions are printed on a single sheet of paper in tiny, blurry font with no clear step numbering. My child and I ended up guessing how things fit together, and every guess was wrong. The final model looks nothing like the picture on the box—it wobbles, leans to one side, and falls apart if you breathe on it.

The advertised "premium sticker sheet" is actually a single sheet of low-tack stickers that refuse to stick to the textured surface. They curl up at the edges within minutes. Worse, the paint used on some of the pieces rubs off on your fingers, leaving a greasy, smudged mess. I tried contacting the seller about a missing part—the little flag that holds the main structure together was simply not in the bag. Their response was a form letter telling me to "double check" and offering a 10% refund, as if my time meant nothing.

I have bought dozens of toys and games on Amazon, and this is the first one that genuinely feels like a scam. It is not just disappointing; it is unsafe for younger kids because of the sharp plastic burrs left on the edges of some pieces that we had to file down ourselves. Save your money and buy a proper puzzle or building set from a brand that cares about quality. This thing is now in the trash, and I regret every penny I spent. I strongly advise you to avoid this product entirely.

text: If you happened upon this book by chance and are looking for some quantitative market insights, then do not be fooled by the books title. From a knowledge perspective the book is worthless. There are plenty of better books on investment theory. Paulos has "regressed to the mean" here. This work merely capitalises on his previous, better efforts. The book is tedious, and in many respects his arguments are fallacious. For example he postulates that if most investors became indexers then markets would cease to be efficient. This is not supported by economic theory, where the contrary holds. It only takes a small number of active investors to retain market efficiency. If you are in search of investment knowledge you will be well served by the author Ron Ross in "Unbeatable Markets". Paulos has not made a contribution here, he has merely compiled a collection of anecdotes from other authors and tried to spin it to make it look like his own. His humour didn't work for me either. If you insist you have to buy the book based on the balance of reader reviews let it be known that you have been warned.

Tired of her father's and the Amish rules, Yoder quickly marries Joseph Lambert, an Amish man who has only recently returned to the Plain way. Long tells Yoder's story of falling in love with her husband and facing her demons. "What the Heart Sees" by Kathleen Fuller tells the story of Ellie Chupp, a young Amish woman who lost her sight as well as her best friend in a horrible accident. When her best friend's former fiance shows up, Ellie's attempts to deal with her disability are disrupted. However, love is just around the corner for Ellie. "Healing Hearts" by Beth Wiseman tells the story of Naaman and Levina Lapp. After 30 years of marriage, they are facing an empty nest, which is something that Naaman especially cannot deal with. He leaves for year, but when he returns he finds that things are not as he hoped they would be. Levina is cold and confused, dealing with whether or not she can trust the man who left her.

I found these three novellas to be enjoyable. Easy to read and interesting, they offer insight to the lives of the Amish, as well as insight into the lives of people in general. The stories are heartwarming and touching, and I would definitely recommend the book.

title: Forget reggaeton, this is Latin alternative at its finest!
text:
Colombian Latin alternative rockeros return to form with this outstanding album. The music is so good you don't even need to understand Spanish to get it. "Complemento," "Paces" and "Al Parque"are sure to appear in a future greatest hits compilation. These musical witch doctors have been concocting just the right amount of rock, Colombian folkloric music, Andean spiritual rhythms and Afro-South American beats for the perfect potion and they've never shared it with anyone (nor has any group been able to reverse engineer it). On "Oye" it's evident they still have the recipe carefully tucked away and the potion still has magical healing powers.

Though their creative trajectory has transformed them from punks to popstars to trip-hopsters (as captured on their appropriately titled and excellent greatest hits CD, "Evolucion/Evolution"), it's the first time they appear to be basking in nostalgia and taking a step back, which isn't necessarily a bad thing if you're the Aterciopelados. And it's especially not a bad thing when the album is reminiscent of their amazing 1997 release, "Pipa de la Paz." Though on this album, you won't catch former uber feminist and vocalist Andrea Echeverri who recently became a mom singing lyrics like: "I won't ruin my silhouette with a baby" as she did on "La Culpable" off the "Pipa" album.

The Latin alternative world can also exhale. Despite the lanky Echeverri and the mousy Hector Buitrago helping each other out on both of their recent solid solo efforts, the rumors ran rampant about an imminent break-up. Though Echeverri's Latin Grammy-nominated album of her same name had a commercial edge over Buitrago's "Connector," Buitrago demonstrated that he can take some calculated artistic risks and still pull off a successful avant-garde album.

To enjoy this album you don't need Spanish. You don't even need an open mind. All you need is good taste. Enjoy! --Mario I. Oña

text:
The Digital Arts & Craft Studio from Fisher-Price is fun for the whole family (I think I used it more the first night than my 3 year old!), but you may be driven crazy by problems with the install process. Buyer beware if you are not willing to troubleshoot potential problems with buggy software.

In my case, I received the "Common Language Runtime Debugging error." If you do too, and your system meets the minimum requirements (and the firmware test, which comes with the software, works) then the problem is most likely your Microsoft .NET Framework installation.

I had 1.1 installed and it appears the program installs both a hotfix and .NET 2.0. To fix: uninstall everything (add/Remove programs). First, the Studio software, then NET 2.0, then the hotfix, and finally NET 1.1. Reboot, and reinstall from the CD. Everything should now work.

Took about an hour, but then we were up and running. Is it worth the money? My toddler is fascinated by the computer, and loves to draw, making this toy the perfect combination to keep her occupied (at least for a little while).

title: Lois good on the counter
text:
I’ve been using the Lois “Good on the Counter” set for about six weeks and overall I’m pleased with the purchase — it’s earned a solid 4 stars from me. I bought it primarily as a functional and attractive way to keep small kitchen items tidy on my countertop, and it delivers on both counts.

The design is simple and modern, which fits nicely with my mostly neutral kitchen. The materials feel sturdy; the weighted base keeps it from tipping when I reach for items, and the finish has held up well to daily use and occasional splashes. Assembly was minimal and straightforward — just a few pieces that snapped together — and the whole unit feels well-made rather than cheap.

Functionally, it’s great for organizing cooking utensils, a couple of fresh fruit, and the stray mail and shopping list that always seems to collect on the counter. The compartments are a good size: deep enough for spatulas and wooden spoons, but not so wide that it dominates the counter. I also appreciate the little non-slip pads on the bottom that protect the surface beneath.

Why not five stars? A couple of small issues. First, the paint finish has started to show faint scuffs where metal utensils rub against it — not a dealbreaker, but noticeable if you look closely. Second, while the size is perfect for my apartment kitchen, it might be a bit small for someone who wants a true catch-all for larger items or a big family’s cooking tools. Finally, the price felt a touch high compared to similar organizers I’ve seen, though the build quality somewhat justifies it.

In short, the Lois counter organizer is a stylish, practical addition to a mid-sized kitchen. It looks good, functions well, and will keep your everyday items within reach — just temper expectations if you need heavy-duty capacity.

text:
I bought this tent for a weekend family camping trip and overall it exceeded my expectations — sturdy, roomy, and well thought out. We’re a family of four (two adults, two kids) and the tent comfortably fit two queen air mattresses plus gear along the perimeter with room to sit. The fabric feels durable and the seams look well sealed; after a night of heavy rain nothing leaked and the ground stayed dry. Ventilation is excellent — the mesh windows and ceiling kept the inside from getting stuffy even in the afternoon heat, and the guy lines and stakes held firm when the wind picked up.

My only serious caveat, and the reason for the title of this review, is setup. Instructions are adequate but the poles and clips require an extra set of hands. I tried to wrestle it up solo and made it more stressful and slower than necessary — there were a few moments where I wished for a partner to help hold corners while I threaded poles. With two people the setup took under 15 minutes. Takeaway: don’t plan to put it up alone if you want a quick, frustration-free start to your outing.

Small touches I appreciated: the vestibule for muddy boots, interior pockets for lights/phones, and the heavy-duty zippers that felt solid. The packed size is reasonable for car camping. If you need a reliable family tent and can have at least two people for setup, this is a great purchase. Highly recommend.

title: A Pop Up Book to Explore with Several Senses
text:
In our family, we have loved pop-up books for several generations, including examples from more than a century ago that are beloved volumes on our bookshelf to this day. While this third book has zero holiday content, we immediately recognized ABC Pop-Up as a marvelous choice for holiday gift-giving.

This pop-up book brilliantly invites adults and children to explore several senses: sound, vision and even tactile experiences of exploring the pop up shapes!

My favorite sequence is a pop-up bed that stands up in front of us, as we read the book, without any immediate clue as to the letters involved. Then, if we closely examine the bed, we discover the pillow has an embossed P in one corner and the quilt has an embossed Q. Little fingers can touch the letters and actually feel the raised shapes.

Then, the sequence continues with a stately tree that leaps up with an attached tire swing and, as we look over the entire page, we discover that we can glimpse the tree’s gnarled roots at the bottom of the page. What letters are we discovering? The tire swing actually dangles from a string and, if our eyes are quick, we can see the S for swing. But what about R? Little fingers can detect an embossed R in the tree’s roots. And then what’s the T? Well, you can guess.

In our family collection, we now own more than 100 pop up books and, while this book is, indeed, little in its physical scale, it is truly a work of genius!

text:
There is a specific topic in this book that I have not seem covered in any of the 25+ book that I have on electromagnetic phenomena. The topic is the shield cut-off frequency of a coaxial cable. Common-mode currents at low frequencies (below a few hundred hertz) cause noise problems with coaxial cables, but signals above tens of kilohertz do not. This is vital data which is apparently not explained in many text books. For me, this topic justifies the cost of the text. Having said that, I am annoyed because the book is quite expensive relative to other books of its size and age. The point is that you have to buy it, but it is expensive to do so.
Even an advanced designer will benefit from this book, although you, like me, won't necessarily want to read all of it. It is sufficient to pick and choose areas of particular interest. The less advanced designer would clearly benefit more and the book would therefore represent better value for them. Given a choice between this one and Morrison's Grounding and Shielding Techniques in Instrumentation, pick this one. This one is more technically accurate and useful.

title: Secret Blade Kubotan ~ very cool
text:
Hey there's not a lot of things you can get for less than 3 bucks these days that will make you think, "cool!" but this little keychain kubotan made me think just that. It's small enough to not be too much of a bother on your actual key ring, but it's big enough to be used as an effective blunt kubotan self defense weapon. But wait, there's more! If you somehow manage to unscrew the bottom cap, spin it around and screw it back on, you have a deadly puncture device that can do some real damage. I say "somehow manage" because I don't think if you found yourself in a dire situation, confronted by someone meaning to do you bodily harm, that you would have the time, steady hand, or patience to get the knife out in time unless you saw the person coming from quite a way off. You need to unscrew the end cap, spin it around and screw it back in with the blade out. It's a neat way to carry a concealed blade but I don't know how it'd fare trying to assemble it in practical application.

The blade itself is not exactly a double-edged knife so much as a thick, very sharply-pointed puncturing device that will leave a hole rather than a slit. If you do manage to stick someone with this thing it'd leave them reeling in pain no matter where you hit. And like I said, blade out or not, it works great as a fist reinforcing kubotan, plus you can use the blunt end to gouge into someone's hand, face, etc. and get them to take a step back so you can make your getaway. It's solid stainless steel and for 3 bucks, it's fully functional. Be careful!

title: Strong opening; a tiresome slog therafter
text: At least one reviewer on this page characterizes SIASL as "juvenile".  I'd have to say that pretty well sums up the greater part of this book.  In its day SIASL may have shone a light on the prevailing counter-cultural trends in American society.  And it may have been cutting edge sci-fi.  As such, it is perhaps of historical interest to those who might be interested.  To the casual reader, however, it's a pretty tiresome read.  The opening section, which deals with the protagonist's arrival on earth and initial adaptation thereto is quite interesting and well-paced.  The greater part of what remains, however, is given over to endless anthropological/religious historical musings of one sort or another, interlaced with endlessly banal descriptions of life in the Utopian commune our hero founds.  Much of this material fails either to titillate the reader's senses or to stimulate his/her intellect.  It reads like one long (LONG) masturbatory exercise on the author's part -- well-written, in fairness, but rather...juvenile.  As for the novel's ending: you'll spot it coming a mile away.  In the final analysis: SIASL is a creature of its times, ill-suited to our own.

title: Great fragrance!  Horrible shampoo!
text:
I really wanted to love this product. The fragrance is absolutely incredible—truly beautiful—a sophisticated, warm, and slightly floral scent that lingers on the skin for hours. If they smell expensive and luxurious, like something you would find in a high-end boutique. I actually bought this specifically because of the reviews raved about the scent, and they were not wrong. I even get compliments from strangers when I wear it. That part is genuinely five stars.

But here is the problem: as a shampoo, it is just terrible. And by that, I mean it is absolutely terrible. I have medium-length, healthy hair that is not particularly demanding hair. It is not color treated or oily or dry. This shampoo leaves my hair feeling like straw. It does not lather well, even with a generous amount. You have to use twice as much as a normal shampoo to feel like you are actually cleaning your scalp. Even then, my hair feels like there is still a weird residue, almost like a waxy coating. After I rinse and condition with my usual conditioner, my hair is tangled and rough. By the time it dries, it is frizzy, dull, and without any movement. It actually looks worse than before I washed it. I tried using it only once a week to see if my hair would adjust, but no change.

I also noticed that my scalp feels tight and itchy after using this. Not immediately, but a few hours later. I thought maybe I was imagining it, but after the fourth try, I had to stop. I have since used it only as a hand wash and body wash in the guest bathroom, which is a shame because I cannot bring myself to throw away a full bottle that cost this much. As a hand soap, it is fine. The scent is lovely on my hands, and it does not dry out my hands the way it does my scalp.

If this product is the ultimate disappointment. A beautiful fragrance trapped in a formula that simply does not work for washing your hair. If the company sold this as a perfume only, I would buy it in a second. But as a shampoo, it is a waste of money. I cannot recommend it for actual hair washing unless you want to follow up with a bad hair day every time. Two stars for the scent, zero stars for performance. Buyer beware.

When it's working, it grinds very well and consistently. But it's fragile and I experienced the "lock-up" issue after the first week or so. It is stressful to clean the grinder because I'm always afraid I'll lock it up when trying to reinsert the bean holder.

I gave it four stars because it's an excellent grinder. The fifth star would've been applied if it wasn't so fragile.

Tips to avoid the lock-up issue:

1) Make sure the clear, rubber part of the burr grinder is facing up before you insert the bean holder.
2) Make sure to align the dot on the bean holder as described in the manual.
3) Be sure the bean holder is all the way seated before turning it to engage.
4) Turn it slowly to make sure it's seated and engaging correctly.

Pros:
- Grinds very well and very consistently.
- Good value for the quality of grind.

Cons:
- Very fragile - will lock up occasionally even if you're very careful.
- Lock-up is permanent and requires a replacement grinder.
- Difficult to clean thoroughly - tedious.

title: A Treasure Trove of Storytelling, Memorable Characters, and Rugged Beauty
text: This is a grand, sweeping, cinematic and sensitive novel about explorations into unmapped Alaskan territory in the 1880s led by a U.S. Army colonel. Concurrent with Col. Forrester's adventure is that of his young wife Sophie, who remains behind at Vancouver Barracks, and takes it upon herself to buck tradition and study the science and art of photography. She is a pioneer in a world where women's lives and roles have long been conscribed; a woman who seeks her own purpose and work, following her love of birds into a means of recording their beauty (and enduring the agonizing months of waiting for her husband's return). The story is told through journal entries, letters, new articles, and excerpts from historical documents which span the time period from the 1880s to the present. Each voice is distinct, credible, and unique. The descriptions of scenery are breathtaking and vivid. One feels the hunger and deprivations, as well as the sweeping grandeur and awe of the terrain, and trepidation surrounding occurrences which defy description. The explorers meet Native peoples who have never before seen white men, yet sense them to be harbingers of ineluctable change. The hardcover contains a treasure trove of illustrations, a magnificent map and many beautiful qualities - well worth the price, as I plan to cherish this book and lend it to trusted friends.

text:
This is the 7th DHMD-210 (or replacement model) we have received in the
past 2-1/2 years: four are currently in use, one failed during warranty
and was replaced with no hassle, two others failed shortly after the warranty expired.
Despite this high failure rate, I still think this is a great little
product for the price. We keep one in our 24' travel trailer, two in my
wife's weaving studios and one in our downstairs family room. The ones
in the family room and in one of the weaving studios are clearly being
pushed beyond their advertised limits for room size, but they pull a lot
of moisture out of the air and we don't want to invest in larger units
for those two spaces so we continue using them and just remember to
empty them frequently. The unit that is in our trailer is unheated and
will occasionally freeze up during the winter; it continues to run but
the vents get covered in ice so no more moisture collects in the water
tank. But we bring it into the house and, after the ice thaws, the unit
resumes normal operation. We'll continue to use this product and
replace them as needed, but now I spend the extra $1 or 2 for the
extended warranty (which I haven't had to use yet). Overall, I would
rate this product as a 4 on a scale of 1-5, 5 being the highest. The
only reason I don't give it a 5 is the high failure rate and not being
able to figure out whether the failure is in the unit itself or in the
power supply so that the entire unit doesn't need to be thrown away when
one fails.

title: Chop Suey Culture
text:
If you like Chinese food, you should read this book. It will tell you everything you should have wondered about chop suey, fortune cookies, the Chinese restaurant industry and the Chinese people who have brought more than food to the United States

Ms. Lee uses her healthy curiosity and excellent research skills to study something we generally take for granted -- Chinese food is so unbiquitous as to be invisible, except when we're hungry. Being the daughter of Chinese immigrants and a New York Times reporter gives Ms. Lee the right lenses for studying her subject and produces insights that are subtle, interesting and thought-provoking. For example: How best to know the actual output of a Chinese restaurant when thinking about buying it? Count the garbage bags in the alley. Why were did Chinese laundries and restaurants survive 19th Century bigotry against the Chinese? Because cooking and washing were women's work and didn't threaten the white male labor force.

Equally as good as Ms. Lee's insights is her writing style. She has a tone that is a bit ironic, a bit whimsical. She appreciates the goofiness of what she is investigating, but also treats the topic respectfully. These are fine balances for a writer to maintain. And she brings many of her points home with a tidy turn of phrase: "Young professionals loved the idea that food could come from a phone rather than a stove." Or, "Common wisdom from one culture is perplexing in another." Or, finally, by describing American soy sauce as a "Frankensauce chemical counterfeit."

However, I was pleasantly surprised to find myself enjoying the books, and the story that revolves around Beka Cooper, George Cooper's ancestor, and guardswoman for the Provost's Guards. It gives a clear picture of the difficulties of the lives of people with no advantages and very little opportunity.

In Bloodhound, Beka is in Port Caynn, searching for the origin of the counterfeited coins that have been popping up in Corus. While the story is enjoyable, the length is not. By page 400, I was wishing that I was at the last page. The end seems to drag on without any resolution. It doesn't help that 'Beka' keeps writing in her diary that she is tired and must stop writing. I would think at her age and maturity, she wouldn't feel the need to write in her diary as if she were talking to it.
The final aspect that was irritating was the very casual, nonchalant way Pounce was disposed of from the list of characters. It was very poorly done, and he was inserted back into the story just as poorly.

As a final thought, would Beka laugh at the irony of knowing that her descendants would have the blood of Trebond as well?

Then a friend recommended these supplements, and I figured it was worth a shot.

The difference was not immediate, but after about ten days I saw him perk up during our morning walk. He started pulling on the leash again, wanting to sniff every bush. Now he plays fetch twice a day and even does this little happy dance when I grab the leash for a walk. The stiffness in his hind legs is much less noticeable, and he jumps onto the couch without that labored groan he used to make.

I also appreciate that these chews have a soft texture, so even a picky older dog like mine takes them without hesitation. They smell like peanut butter, not medicine, and the ingredients list includes glucosamine and turmeric, which I know are good for joint health. I was worried about potential side effects, but he has had no digestive issues whatsoever.

Overall, this product has given my senior dog a new lease on life. He is moving better, playing more, and seems genuinely happier. For the price, the results have been fantastic. I will definitely be buying more and have already recommended them to my neighbor with a similar issue. Highly recommend for any dog that seems to be slowing down with age.

title: Afghanistan through the eyes of a child
text: A war-torn country plagued by violence.  An 11-year-old girl forced to risk her life and save her family. These are the realities in Deborah Ellis' novel "The Breadwinner" (Groundwood Books 2000).  Told from young Parvana's perspective, the story focuses on her family of six living in Kabul, Afghanistan.  After the Taliban take control of their city, Parvana's family is forced out of their large home by a bomb explosion and into a one-room apartment.  The women are removed from school and forced to stay in the house unless escorted by a male.  When Parvana's father is arrested because he attended university in England, their family must make the tough decision to have her pose as a boy in order to leave the house and work in the marketplace to earn money for food.  While working, Parvana runs into Shauzia, a girl she knew from school who is also posing as a boy to support her family. They start to work together and soon become close friends, encountering a number of sobering, scary situations along the way. Though children may not experience the same life, they will no doubt relate to Parvana's story and her arguments with her older sister, unfairness of chore responsibilities, and love for her family.  The Breadwinner is not a happy story with a happy conclusion, but one that will leave the reader with a different view of Afghanistan, as seen through the eyes of a child.  An author's note and glossary of terms serve as a helpful aide in introducing children to the history and culture of Afghanistan.

text:
What makes this collection unique: it's printed on full-size newspaper stock
What makes this really amazing: they have taken the actual page from the newspaper of that year and reprinted it here with the ads and other articles as originally in the newspaper. You may find yourself ignoring the crossword and reading, say, the movie or book review from 1990. Or just perusing the ads.

The editors have taken one puzzle from each year back to 1942 and printed its entire page.

The downside to the book so far (I started at 2016 and worked backwards) is when you get to the Eugene Maleska years (77-93) (Oh, let me
correct myself: it's Eugene T. Maleska, not to be confused with all those other Eugene Maleska's in the USA). That "T" might tell you all you
need to know about his puzzles. They reek of what passed for knowledge way back when: obscure Broadway shows, "great" writers that most
people have never heard of, French language (by the way, there was an error in one of those), capitols of regions of small nations etc.

I have another compilation of NY Times puzzles that goes back decades which is very challenging because what passed for common knowledge back then is obscure now. However, that's not my issue with Maleska.

Altogether, this is a great gift for any crossword puzzler; mine was a gift as well.

title: Audience
text:
I finished reading Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer’s book titled, The Authority of the Court and the Peril of Politics, thinking about his intended audience. If his audience is the informed American citizen, his claims of the court not being political come across as naïve. If his audience is his fellow justices and his message is for them not to overreach because they may find the authority of the court diminished, that made a bit more sense to me. I thought of Alan Greenspan’s confession about his foundational error in the runup to the financial crisis. He assumed that banks would act prudently as a form of self-preservation. As we know, they didn’t. Why Breyer might expect fellow justices to preserve the authority of the Supreme Court by not overreaching in their decisions, I can’t imagine. We will all watch the exercise of power and learn how much peril can be absorbed by our democratic republic.

title: Digital Babylon and Faithful Christians
text:
We live in a digital world, and one in which it seems Christians are swimming against the tide. Those who are coming to Christ in their youth within the digital age are often finding themselves lost in the sea. While following Jesus hasn't changed since Paul, it does look different from generation to generation. In an age of instant connection, limitless information, and constant entertainment, all filled with a value system that opposes God, "Faith for Exiles" asks the question of how we can create lasting disciples within this digital Babylon. In the digital age, "the goal of discipleship is to develop Jesus followers who are resiliently faithful in the face of cultural coercion and who live a vibrant life in the Spirit." David Kinnaman, president of @barnagroup, and @mattmatlock present 5 practices for Christians in the digital age.
•
1. Intimacy with Jesus to form resilient identity. Does Jesus bring you joy? Is worship a lifestyle? Is Scripture relevant to your life? Is your relationship with Jesus personal and intimate?
2. Develop muscles of cultural discernment. Is the Bible teaching at your church relevant to your life? Do you receive wisdom on how to live in a secular age? Is your worldview Christian?
3. Form meaningful, intergenerational friendships. Do you feel like you belong at church? IS someone encouraging you spiritually? Do you have personal close friends at church?
4.Train for vocational discipleship. Do you use your unique talents to honor God? Do you recognize God's unique calling on your life? Do you serve others in your church?
5. Engage in countercultural mission. Do you desire for others to see Jesus reflected in your life? Do you feel a responsibility to tell others about Jesus? Does the mission of the Church excite you?
•
This book seeks to create resilient individuals who cling to the truths of who they are in Christ, their purpose on earth, and the ways we serve and evangelize others. This book is packed front to back with research, statistics, diagrams, and charts. But the true fruit of the book comes in the theological insight and assessment of the next gen. The entire book is also gorgeously designed thanks to @chazrusso. **book graciously provided by Baker Books for an honest review

The padding is far too thin for a medium-sized dog. Within a few days, the stuffing shifted to the sides, leaving a hard spot in the middle that is essentially just the floor. I noticed my dog would get settled in, but after about ten minutes, he would stand up and pace around, unable to find a comfortable position. He eventually gave up on this bed entirely and went back to sleeping on a old bath mat.

I suspect the sizing is off or the foam quality is just low grade. It feels more like a decorative pillow than an actual supportive pet bed. For the price I paid, I expected something that could actually support a dog's weight without flattening instantly. It is a shame because the fabric is nice and it is easy to clean, but the primary purpose of a dog bed is comfort, and this product fails in that department. I would not recommend this for any dog over ten pounds, as they will just sink right through to the hardwood. I will be returning this and looking for something with actual memory foam instead of this cheap filler.

The magnets on these are very strong and requires more than a little tug to disconnect them. One concern I had was "Would I get shocked by the part that remains in the laptop?" title: Not as sticky or strong as Reel/Related Products brand flatback, but will do as a 2nd choice.
text:
Compared to Reel/Related Products Inc flatback tape, Intertape 530 utility-grade is an okay 2nd choice. Maybe I need to try a different grade of Intertape - this being the utility grade - but so far I'm a little underwhelmed.
Intertape is 7.2 mil thick, but my old tape - Reel brand - is 7.4. Doesn't seem like much, but you can tell the difference. I question the Intertape 45 lb tensile strength claim. Reel tape says it's strength is only 32 lb, but it is tougher tape. It takes intentional effort to tear Reel tape, but Intertape tears very readily. Could be handy - if that's what you're after. If you need a lot of tensile strength in your tape, definitely go with the Reel brand.
Intertape definitely has less adhesive, but some people might find this a plus. You can reposition it - if you do it right away. Reel tape is very sticky and once it is down, it is down - you know you have a good, solid bond immediately.
I can't find Reel brand flatback retail, so I guess we'll have to settle.

text: [[VIDEOID:5c6d3d8de2254fa104eb8cfc6103cfda]] I’m a hairstylist and I do exstensions on a regular basis. The bundles are VERY thin I ordered body wave 16/18/20. Typically 4 tracks is more than enough hair for me. The hair feels like plastic hair but it didn’t melt when I curled it on high heat. I’ve washed it once. It doesn’t really hold color. I’ve had it installed for 5 days, I haven’t seen much shedding since the first day and haven’t had any tangles yet. If you’re making a wig I don’t think the 3 bundles would even be enough to make it look full.
